chapter: New York, Nick's and the Army
title: Learning the New Orleans repertoire at Nick's
summary: Chicago played pop tunes in Dixieland style but Nick's wanted Muskrat Ramble and Alligator Crawl; Brad Gowans writes out the leads for him.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: All right - well, now, tell me-- tell the story about the fact that, at this point, you didn't really know what you called the Old New Orleans chestnut.
But, they played a lot of that stuff.
This is where the old thing - the critics come up with and if you played Dixie Land in Chicago - it was different than Dixie Land in New York or in New

Orleans. Now, the kind of Dixie Land and they were playing at Nick's and you could not play anything else but -- Dixie Land at Nick's -- now, in Chicago, we played Dixie Land with the pop songs of the day; what was ever popular --

We turned it into a Dixie Land--- when you get to New York and they were playing the "Muskrat Ramble" and the "Alligator Crawl" and they were playing all these old songs from New Orleans, I didn't know them--- you know, I just didn't know them. So, ---

Yes, but I stayed there a very short time and tried to fake my way through some of those arrangements, which I got by ear quickly and, then, Brunis left--- now, I don't remember just what Brunis did at that time -- but he left and Brad Gowans came in and he wrote out for me the lead to every Dixie Land sound you could think of that ever was made and I was home free then; I could just look at the part and play my part---
